source_text:
Nec saltem de praesentibus capitis experimentum, quam uos inritae pollicitationis cassa uota decipiant: quid post mortem inpendeat, miseri,-dum adhuc uiuitis, aestimate.
ecce pars uestrum, et maior, melior, ut dicitis, egetis algetis, opere fame laboratis, et Deus patitur dissimulat, non uult aut non potest opitulari suis: ita aut inualidus aut iniquus est.
tn, qui inmortalitatem postumam somnias, cum periculo quateris, cum febribus ureris, cum dolore laceraris, nondum condicionem tuam sentis? nondum adgnoscis fragilitatem ? inuitus miser infirmitatis argueris nec fateris.
sed omitto communia. ecce uobis minae, supplicia, tormenta, et iam non adorandae sed subeundae cruces, ignes etiam quos et praedicitis et timetis: ubi deus ille, qui subuenire reuiuescentibus potest, uiuentibus non potest?
nonne Romani sine uestro deo imperant regnant, fruuntur orbe toto uestrique dominantur? uos uero suspensi interim atque solliciti honestis uoluptatibus abstinetis, non spectacula uisitis, non pompis interestis, conuiuia publica absque uobis, sacra certamina, praecerptos cibos et delibatos altaribus potus abhorretis. sic reformidatis deos quos negatis.
non floribus caput nectitis, non corpus odoribus honestatis: reseruatis unguenta funeribus, coronas etiam sepulcris denegatis, pallidi trepidi, misericordia digni, sed nostrorum deorum. ita nec resurgitis miseri nec interim uiuitis.
proinde si quid sapientiae uobis ant uerecundiae est, desinite caeli plagas et mundi fata et secreta rimari: satis est pro pedibus aspicere maxime indoctis, inpolitis, rudibus, agrestibus, quibus non est datum intellegere ciuilia, multo magis denegatum est disserere diuina.
thought_title: The misery and impotence of Christians
orientation: Caecilius is still attacking Christianity, now turning from the absurdity of resurrection to the present wretchedness of Christians and their absent God.
pass_a_gloss: And at least take an experiment from present things, how the empty prayers of a vain promise deceive you: what hangs over you after death, wretched ones, while you still live, estimate. Look, a part of you, and the greater part, the better part, as you say, are in need, are cold, labor in work and hunger, and God suffers it, ignores it, does not wish or is not able to help his own: thus he is either weak or unjust. You, who dream of immortality after death, when you are shaken with danger, when you burn with fevers, when you are torn with pain, do you not yet feel your condition? Do you not yet recognize your frailty? Unwilling, wretched one, you are convicted of weakness and you do not confess it. But I pass over common things. Look, for you there are threats, punishments, tortures, and now crosses not to be adored but to be endured, fires also which you both predict and fear: where is that god, who is able to help those reviving, but is not able to help the living? Do not the Romans without your god rule, reign, enjoy the whole world and lord it over your people? You indeed, suspended meanwhile and anxious, abstain from honorable pleasures, you do not visit the spectacles, you are not present at the processions, public banquets are without you, the sacred contests, you abhor foods taken beforehand and drinks tasted at the altars. Thus you dread the gods whom you deny. You do not wreathe your head with flowers, you do not honor your body with perfumes: you reserve ointments for funerals, you even deny garlands to tombs, pale, trembling, worthy of pity, but of the pity of our gods. Thus neither do you rise again, wretched ones, nor do you live in the meantime. Therefore if you have any wisdom or modesty, cease to examine the regions of heaven and the fates and secrets of the world: it is enough to look before your feet, especially for the unlearned, the unpolished, the rude, the rustic, to whom it is not given to understand civil matters, much more is it denied to discuss divine matters.

choices.why: cassus means vain or empty; uota here are the prayers or vows Christians make in hope of resurrection, which Caecilius calls futile.

choices.english: a part of you, and the greater part, the better part
choices.why: Caecilius mockingly echoes the Christian claim that the poor and suffering are the better part of their community.
rejected: most of you, the better sort

choices.why: dissimulo means to pretend not to notice, to overlook deliberately; here God is accused of turning a blind eye to Christian suffering.
subeundae is a gerundive of obligation; Caecilius contrasts the Christian adoration of the cross with the actual crosses they must undergo as punishment.
suspensi conveys being held in suspense, uncertain of the future; interim stresses that while they wait for the afterlife they are miserable now.

choices.term: praecerptos cibos et delibatos altaribus potus
choices.english: foods taken beforehand and drinks tasted at the altars
choices.why: praecerptos means plucked or taken before the offering, delibatos means tasted or sampled; both refer to sacrificial food and drink Christians refuse.
rejected: foods snatched beforehand and drinks sipped at altars

pass_b_english: You do not even learn a lesson from what is before you, from how empty vows and hollow promises deceive you. Miserable people, while you are still alive, consider what hangs over you after death.

Look at a part of you—and the greater part, the better part, as you say. You are in need, you are cold, you labor in hunger, and God ignores it. He does not want to help his own, or he cannot. So he is either weak or unjust.

You who dream of immortality after death—when you are shaken by danger, when you burn with fever, when you are torn by pain, do you not yet feel your condition? Do you not yet recognize your fragility? Unwilling and miserable, you are convicted of weakness, and you will not admit it.

But I pass over what is common to everyone. Look at what awaits you: threats, punishments, tortures, and crosses now not to be adored but to be endured, and the fires you both predict and fear. Where is that God who can help those rising again but cannot help the living?

Do not the Romans rule and reign without your God, enjoy the whole world, and lord it over you? But you, suspended meanwhile and anxious, abstain from honorable pleasures. You do not visit the shows, you do not attend the processions, public banquets go on without you, sacred games, foods snatched first and drinks tasted at the altars you abhor. So you dread the gods you deny.

You do not weave flowers around your head, you do not honor your body with perfumes. You reserve ointments for funerals, you even deny garlands to tombs, pale and trembling, worthy of pity from our gods. So you neither rise again, miserable ones, nor do you live in the meantime.

Therefore, if you have any wisdom or modesty, stop prying into the plagues of heaven, the fates of the world and its secrets. It is enough to look at what is before your feet, especially for the untaught, the uncultured, the rude, the rustic, who have not been given to understand civil matters, and much more have been denied the right to discuss divine ones.

problems.quote: stop prying into the regions of heaven and the fates and secrets of the world
problems.source_quote: desinite caeli plagas et mundi fata et secreta rimari
problems.why: Latin “plagas” means plagues/misfortunes, not “regions of heaven”.
problems.fix: stop prying into the plagues of heaven, the fates of the world and its secrets

problems.why: Latin adds only “but of our gods”, not “pity”. The word “pity” is not in the source.
praecerptos means 'snatched beforehand' or 'torn away first' as sacrificial portions, not merely 'taken beforehand'.
problems.ruling: praecerptos cibos = ‘snatched/seized foods’, not merely ‘taken beforehand’, losing sense of force

edits.old: stop prying into the regions of heaven and the fates and secrets of the world
edits.new: stop prying into the plagues of heaven, the fates of the world and its secrets

edits.old: worthy of pity—but of our gods' pity
edits.new: worthy of pity—but of our gods

fixed: Changed 'regions of heaven' to 'plagues of heaven' per source 'caeli plagas'.
Removed 'pity' after 'our gods' per source 'sed nostrorum deorum'.
Changed 'taken beforehand' to 'snatched first' per source 'praecerptos'.

problems.quote: You do not even take a test from the present
problems.source_quote: Nec saltem de praesentibus capitis experimentum
problems.why: English loses Caecilius's sarcastic 'capitis' (of your head/life); but more importantly, this is Caecilius mocking Christians, and 'you' should convey his hostile tone
problems.fix: You don't even take a test from present things
problems.ruling: Translation omits capitis (head/life) and sarcastic tone, altering the intended mockery.

edits.old: You do not even take a test from the present
edits.new: You do not even take a test from present things

fixed: The English 'from the present' loses the source's 'de praesentibus' (from present things), which Caecilius uses to mock Christians' failure to learn from their own circumstances. Changed to 'from present things' to match the source while keeping the sarcastic tone.

problems.fix: who can help those rising again but cannot help the living?
problems.ruling: Latin 'reuiuescentibus' = those revived/resurrected; English 'reviving' misstates as ongoing action.

problems.quote: worthy of pity—but of our gods
problems.why: Sed governs both phrases: 'worthy of pity from our gods,' not contrastive 'but.'
problems.fix: worthy of pity from our gods
problems.ruling: 'sed nostrorum deorum' means 'but (only) to our gods'; translation 'but of our gods' omits the limiting sense.

problems.why: Latin says 'cassa uota' (empty vows/promises), not prayers.
problems.ruling: cassa uota = 'empty wishes/vows', not prayers; orare/deprecari = pray. Meaning shifted.

edits.old: who can help the reviving but cannot help the living?
edits.new: who can help those rising again but cannot help the living?

edits.old: worthy of pity—but of our gods
edits.new: worthy of pity from our gods

fixed: Changed 'reviving' to 'those rising again' to match 'reuiuescentibus' (rising again/resurrected).
Changed 'worthy of pity—but of our gods' to 'worthy of pity from our gods' because 'sed' governs both phrases, meaning 'worthy of pity from our gods,' not contrastive.
Changed 'empty prayers' to 'empty vows' to match 'cassa uota' (empty vows/promises), not prayers.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Octavius suddenly calls Caecilius 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks it's a new person.
problems.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.

problems.quote: blind fortune or uncertain nature rules
problems.why: These terms shift between Caecilius's skeptical 'fortune/nature' and Octavius's theological 'fate' without clear distinction of who uses which.
problems.fix: Clarify that 'fate' is God's ordering, 'fortune' is blind chance.

problems.quote: You do not even take a test from present things
problems.why: 'take a test' is not idiomatic; means 'learn a lesson' or 'draw proof.'
problems.fix: 'You do not even draw proof from present things'

edits.old: You do not even take a test from present things
edits.new: You do not even draw proof from present things

fixed: The 'Natalis' problem is not present in this section; no edit needed.
The 'fate/fortune' problem is not present in this section; no edit needed.
Changed 'take a test' to 'draw proof' to match the source's 'capitis experimentum' (take an experiment/proof).

dismissed.quote: and God ignores it. He does not want to help his own, or he cannot.
dismissed.why: Latin says God pretends (dissimulat) that he does not want or cannot help, implying deceit; English says God ignores, changing the nature of God's behavior.
dismissed.note: 'patitur dissimulat' means God lets it happen and looks away, so 'ignores it' is fair. The proposed 'pretends that he does not want' misparses the Latin.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening phrase as 'learn a lesson from what is before you,' made the speaker's address to Christians explicit, and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every claim, qualification, and scriptural reference.

notes.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.
